summary: Describes a heartbeat mechanism between the mobile access gateway and the local mobility anchor in Proxy Mobile IPv6. It detects failures and tells peers quickly when a node recovers, so they can act. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Two helpers keep sending each other a quick are you there, so each knows soon when the other stops answering.

questions: how does an lma detect mag failure
what is the restart counter in pmipv6
subtitle: A periodic are-you-there message between Proxy Mobile IPv6 gateways and anchors, plus a counter that reveals restarts.

tldr.problem: In a Proxy Mobile IPv6 domain, mobile access gateways and local mobility anchors need a consistent view of each other's reachability, and need to learn quickly when a peer has restarted and lost its state.
tldr.mechanism: The two peers exchange Heartbeat Request and Response messages every HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL seconds, matched by sequence number. A Restart Counter option in the response reveals when a peer rebooted and lost session state.
tldr.outcome: A node that sees too many missing responses concludes its peer is unreachable, and a changed Restart Counter means the peer crashed and recovered. What to do about it is left to the implementation.

today: RFC 5847 is a Proposed Standard from June 2010 and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the specification of the PMIPv6 heartbeat between a MAG and an LMA.

sections.title: Why a Heartbeat
sections.content:
In Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6, RFC 5213), a mobile access gateway (MAG) acts as a proxy for Mobile IPv6 signaling, and a local mobility anchor (LMA) anchors a mobile node's sessions. They set up a bidirectional tunnel for all of the mobile nodes' data traffic.

In such a distributed setting the nodes need two things: a consistent idea of whether each other is reachable, and a quick way to learn that a peer has recovered from a failure. If an LMA restarts, for example, the MAG should learn of it quickly so it can take appropriate action, such as releasing resources.

This document adds a Heartbeat message (a Mobility Header message) exchanged periodically, or sent unsolicited soon after a restart. It does not specify what a node does in response to what it learns.
sections.plainLanguage: When many helpers work together, each needs to know if the others are still around, and to find out fast if one of them fell asleep and lost its notes.

sections.title: Requests, Responses and Failure Detection
sections.content:
The MAG and the LMA exchange Heartbeat messages every HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL seconds. Each side can start an exchange. Every Heartbeat Request carries a sequence number that increases monotonically, and the response is matched to it.

A request can be sent only while there is at least one proxy Binding Cache entry for a mobile node attached to that MAG. If there is none, the message SHOULD NOT be sent. A PMIPv6 node MUST answer every Heartbeat Request with a Heartbeat Response, whether or not it has an active Binding Cache entry.

Before sending the next request, a node increments a local counter MISSING_HEARTBEAT if the previous request went unanswered. When it exceeds MISSING_HEARTBEATS_ALLOWED, the node concludes the peer is not reachable. Any response resets the counter.

A node that does not support Heartbeat answers with a Binding Error with status 2 (unrecognized MH type). The sender MUST NOT use Heartbeat with that peer again. A node that detects a failed or restarted peer that kept no session state should mark the related binding update list or binding cache entries as invalid.
sections.plainLanguage: Every so often you ask 'still there?'. If a few asks in a row go unanswered, you decide your friend is gone. Answers always have to be given, even if you have nothing to talk about.

sections.title: Detecting Restarts
sections.content:
Each PMIPv6 node MUST keep a monotonically increasing Restart Counter. It is incremented every time the node reboots and loses PMIPv6 session state, and not when it recovers without losing state. The counter MUST survive reboots. The node reports it in a Restart Counter option in each Heartbeat Response.

Each node also MUST store the counter of every peer it has sessions with, though those stored values need not survive reboots. When a response arrives with a different value than before, the receiver assumes the peer crashed and recovered, and stores the new value.

A node that restarts and loses session state SHOULD send an unsolicited Heartbeat Response with an incremented counter to all peers it had sessions with, so they learn quickly. This is possible only if it can store peer information across reboots. The sequence number in such a message is ignored and no response is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Each helper wears a badge with a number that goes up every time they wake up with a blank memory. When a friend sees a new number, they know to start over.

sections.title: The Heartbeat Message Format
sections.content:
The Heartbeat is a Mobility Header message (RFC 3775) with the MH Type field set to 13. After the Mobility Header checksum come a Reserved area, two flag bits, a 32-bit Sequence Number and mobility options.

  • R: 0 for a request, 1 for a response.
  • U: 1 in an unsolicited Heartbeat Response, otherwise 0.
  • Mobility options: zero or more TLV options. A receiver MUST ignore and skip options it does not understand.

The Restart Counter mobility option, the only valid option in this message, is valid only in a Heartbeat Response. Its Type MUST be 28, its Length is 4, and it holds a 32-bit counter. It has an alignment requirement of 4n+2.

If the network between the MAG and LMA is IPv4-only, the Mobility Header is carried inside UDP in an IPv4 packet as specified in RFC 5844.
sections.plainLanguage: The message is a tiny form with a tick box for 'question or answer', a tick box for 'I just woke up', a number to match answers to questions, and room for the badge number.

sections.title: Configuration Variables
sections.content:
Both nodes must let two variables be configured. HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL is the time in seconds between two consecutive requests. Its default is 60 seconds, and it SHOULD NOT be set below 30 seconds or above 3600 seconds. Sending too often can add overhead on the path and cause congestion; a larger value reduces the burden.

MISSING_HEARTBEATS_ALLOWED is the maximum number of consecutive requests that may go unanswered before the peer is declared unreachable. Its default is 3.
sections.plainLanguage: You choose how often to ask 'still there?', and how many missed answers you will put up with before you give up on a friend.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Heartbeats only check reachability and carry nothing useful to an eavesdropper, so confidentiality protection is not required. Integrity protection with IPsec (RFC 4301) MUST be supported on the MAG and the LMA. The Heartbeat is another subtype of the Mobility Header already protected by IPsec under RFC 5213, so the same mechanisms apply, with the security policy entries using the new MH Type as selector. If dynamic key negotiation is needed, IKEv2 (RFC 4306) should be used.
sections.plainLanguage: The 'still there?' call is not secret, but it must not be forged, so it is sealed the same way as the other messages between the helpers.
